pattern: Time-triggered work at scale: index work by its due time, give each partition exactly one leased owner that claims and advances in one transaction, decouple execution through a queue with visibility timeouts, and make at-least-once safe with deterministic idempotency keys, backoff and a dead-letter queue.

tips.nudge: What does a user hand to this system?
tips.hint: Write a requirement for registering one-off and recurring jobs.
tips.show: F1: Schedule a job one-off (run_at / delay) or recurring (cron), with handler and payload; pause, edit, cancel.

tips.nudge: What must happen when a job's time arrives?
tips.hint: Add a requirement for executing jobs on time on workers.
tips.show: F2: Execute each job at its scheduled time on a pool of workers.

tips.nudge: Jobs fail. What does the user expect then?
tips.hint: Add a requirement for retries and what happens after the last one.
tips.show: F3: Retry failed runs with backoff up to N attempts, then dead-letter them.

tips.nudge: How does an owner find out whether last night's job ran?
tips.hint: Add a requirement for run status and history.
tips.show: F4: Show status and history of every run for 30 days.

tips.nudge: A worker crashes halfway through a job. Is the run lost, repeated or neither?
tips.hint: State the delivery guarantee as a non-functional requirement.
tips.show: N2: at-least-once execution; no run is lost when a node dies; duplicates made harmless with idempotency.

tips.nudge: How late may a 09:00 job start?
tips.hint: State a timing target, including busy moments.
tips.show: N1: start within 2 s of scheduled time (p99), including top-of-the-hour spikes.

tips.nudge: Start from runs per day.
tips.hint: dispatches/s = runs per day / 86,400.
tips.show: avg_dispatch_qps = 100M / day ≈ 1,160 /s.

tips.nudge: Everyone loves '0 * * * *'. What does that do to the rate at :00?
tips.hint: Multiply the average rate by a burst factor for the top of the hour.
tips.show: peak_dispatch_qps = 1,160 × 10 ≈ 12,000 /s at the top of the hour.

tips.nudge: Every run leaves a record. How many, for how long, how big?
tips.hint: storage = runs per day × retention days × bytes per run record.
tips.show: run_history_storage_30d = 100M × 30 × 500 B ≈ 1.5 TB.

tips.nudge: Which call registers a job?
tips.hint: A POST taking the schedule, handler, payload and retry policy.
tips.show: POST /jobs {name, schedule: cron | run_at, handler, payload, retry_policy, timeout} → 201 {job_id, next_run_at}

tips.nudge: How does a user see what happened to their job?
tips.hint: A GET that lists a job's runs with their status.
tips.show: GET /jobs/{id}/runs?status&from → [{run_id, scheduled_at, attempt, status, error}]

checks.label: Job definition modelled for fast due lookup

tips.nudge: What field lets the system ask 'what is due now' cheaply?
tips.hint: Store each job with an explicit next fire time that can be indexed.
tips.show: jobs(job_id PK, schedule, next_run_at (indexed), handler, payload, retry_policy, status, version).

checks.label: Job storage designed as its own part

tips.nudge: Where do 50M definitions live so you can both edit them and ask 'what's due'?
tips.hint: Add a part for the job store: compare a key-value store with indexed SQL.
tips.show: Part 'Job definitions and the schedule store': Postgres partitioned by hash(job_id) with an index on next_run_at.

checks.label: Finding due jobs designed as its own part

tips.nudge: Scanning 50M rows every second is a non-starter. What do you read instead?
tips.hint: Add a part for finding due jobs: compare a full scan, an indexed range per partition, a priority queue and time buckets.
tips.show: Part 'Finding due jobs': leased schedulers per partition run SELECT … WHERE next_run_at <= now()+5s … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

checks.label: Execution guarantees designed as their own part

tips.nudge: An executor dies at minute 20 of a 30-minute job. How does anyone find out?
tips.hint: Add a part for dispatch and execution: compare direct calls, a queue with leases and 'exactly once'.
tips.show: Part 'Dispatch and execution': queue with visibility timeout and heartbeats; Idempotency-Key = job_id + scheduled_at.

checks.label: Failure handling designed as its own part

tips.nudge: A downstream API is down for an hour. What do your retries do to it?
tips.hint: Add a part for retries and dead letters, and how owners see what happened.
tips.show: Part 'Retries, dead letters and status': exponential backoff + jitter via next_run_at, DLQ after max attempts, job_runs history.

tips.nudge: Should the component that decides *when* also be the one that runs the job?
tips.hint: Put a buffer between the scheduler and a pool of workers that pull from it.
tips.show: Schedulers → run queue (visibility timeout) → executor pool.

checks.label: Permanently failing work has somewhere to go

tips.nudge: What happens to a job that fails every single time?
tips.hint: Add a place to park runs that exhausted their retries.
tips.show: A dead-letter queue, with a triage worker that alerts the owner and can redrive runs.

tips.nudge: Your guarantee allows a run to happen twice. Who makes that safe?
tips.hint: Decide how duplicates are detected or neutralised.
tips.show: Deterministic run_id = job_id + scheduled_at passed as an Idempotency-Key; conditional status updates per attempt.

checks.label: Burst at the top of the hour handled

tips.nudge: 12,000 jobs want to start at 09:00:00. What do you do?
tips.hint: Decide how the system absorbs or smooths the burst.
tips.show: Claim a few seconds ahead, let the queue absorb, autoscale executors on queue depth, and offer opt-in jitter.

tips.nudge: What gets written on every single run?
tips.hint: Walk the dispatch path and name what saturates first.
tips.show: The jobs store (next_run_at advanced per run), per-partition polling at :00, and executor slots held by slow handlers.

tips.nudge: Kill a scheduler, an executor and a handler in turn. What happens each time?
tips.hint: Name each failure and how the design recovers.
tips.show: Scheduler: lease expires, another takes the partition. Executor: visibility timeout re-queues. Handler: backoff, then DLQ.
